content: 1. All children with severe acute malnutrition are at risk of hypoglycemia. Upon admission, they should immediately receive a feed or a 10% glucose or sucrose solution. Frequent feeding every 2 hours is critical. Blood glucose levels should be measured immediately, and hypoglycemia is diagnosed when blood glucose is less than 3 mmol/L (54 mg/dL). If blood glucose cannot be measured, assume hypoglycemia and initiate treatment. 2. For treatment of hypoglycemia, administer 50 mL of a 10% glucose or sucrose solution orally or via a nasogastric tube, followed by the first feed as soon as possible. If the child is unconscious, provide intravenous (IV) 10% glucose at 5 mL/kg. If IV access is not feasible, administer the glucose or sucrose solution via a nasogastric tube. In the absence of IV glucose, sublingual administration of sugar moistened with water can be used, repeating every 20 minutes to prevent relapse. 3. Monitor the child for early swallowing difficulties, which may delay absorption. If this occurs, administer another dose of sugar. Continue oral or nasogastric feeding every 2 hours to prevent recurrence of hypoglycemia. Start appropriate IV or intramuscular (IM) antibiotics as needed. 4. If the initial blood glucose was low, repeat the measurement after 30 minutes. If blood glucose falls below 3 mmol/L again, repeat the 10% glucose or oral sugar solution. Monitor for signs of deterioration, such as a drop in consciousness or worsening hypoglycemia, and treat accordingly. 5. Hypothermia is common in malnourished children and often indicates coexisting hypoglycemia or serious infection. Hypothermia is diagnosed when the axillary temperature is below 35°C (95°F) or does not register on a standard thermometer. 6. Treat hypothermia by addressing hypoglycemia and infection. Feed the child immediately and every 2 hours unless abdominal distension is present. If dehydrated, rehydrate first. Re-warm the child by ensuring they are clothed, covering them with a warmed blanket, and using a heater or lamp nearby (not directed at the child). Alternatively, use skin-to-skin contact with the mother, covering both with a warmed blanket. 7. Keep the child away from drafts and ensure they are covered at all times, especially at night. Use a warm bonnet to reduce heat loss. Check for hypoglycemia whenever hypothermia is detected. Avoid bathing very ill children and ensure wet clothing or bedding is replaced to keep the child dry. 8. Dehydration in malnourished children should be assumed in cases of watery diarrhea or reduced urine output. Rehydrate slowly using oral or nasogastric rehydration with ReSoMal (rehydration solution for malnutrition) at 5–10 mL/kg per hour for up to 12 hours. Avoid IV rehydration unless the child is in shock. 9. Monitor the progress of rehydration every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, then hourly for the next 4–10 hours. Signs of successful rehydration include reduced respiratory and pulse rates, the return of tears, moist mouth, less sunken eyes, and improved skin turgor. Be vigilant for signs of overhydration, such as increased respiratory or pulse rates, and stop rehydration immediately if these occur. 10. All severely malnourished children have deficiencies in potassium and magnesium, which may take up to 2 weeks to correct. Edema is partly due to potassium deficiency and sodium retention. Do not treat edema with diuretics. Provide extra potassium (3–4 mmol/kg/day) and magnesium (0.4–0.6 mmol/kg/day) by adding them to feeds during preparation. 11. All severely malnourished children should be assumed to have an infection upon hospital admission and treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately. Hypoglycemia and hypothermia are often signs of severe infection. If specific infections such as pneumonia or dysentery are identified, treat with appropriate antibiotics. 12. In areas with high HIV prevalence, children with severe acute malnutrition should be tested for HIV to determine the need for antiretroviral therapy (ART). If HIV-positive, initiate ART as soon as possible after stabilizing metabolic complications and sepsis. Monitor closely for the first 6–8 weeks for metabolic complications and opportunistic infections. 13. Micronutrient deficiencies are universal in severely malnourished children. Do not give iron initially, as it can worsen infections. Wait until the child has a good appetite and starts gaining weight, usually in the second week, before starting iron supplementation. Multivitamins, including vitamin A, folic acid, zinc, and copper, are already included in therapeutic feeds like F-75 and F-100. 14. Initial refeeding should be gradual. Use F-75 therapeutic milk at 130 mL/kg/day (or 100 mL/kg/day for children with severe edema). Feed every 2 hours initially, then every 3 hours as the child stabilizes. Encourage continued breastfeeding alongside prescribed formula amounts. 15. Monitor feeding progress and adjust volumes gradually. For children with persistent diarrhea, consider using cereal-based F-75, which has lower osmolality but requires cooking. Feed weak children using a spoon, dropper, or syringe. Transition to catch-up feeding with F-100 formula once the child is stabilized and gaining weight.
